title: Germany's far-right AfD party copied Trump's playbook and won. It now hopes to use it to govern
summary: From creating a deportation task force to revising history lessons in schools, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which won a resounding victory in the state of Saxony-Anhlat last…

image.caption: A supporter attends an election campaign event for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in a borough of Berlin in July. The Berlin state election is on Sunday and the AfD is polling in third place. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Christian Machek is at a rally for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Berlin. Despite backing a nationalist party thousands of kilometres from the United States, he considers himself both an AfD and "Trump supporter."

The AfD secured a resounding victory in a recent regional election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the party is designated as right-wing extremist by the local domestic intelligence agency.
U.S. President Donald Trump celebrated the win on social media.

"I was happy [Trump] congratulated the AfD for a good campaign," said Machek, an Austrian Belgian citizen who lives in Berlin and says he works with the party in Germany’s parliament, the Bundestag, as an assistant to its spokesperson on religious affairs.
Ahead of Sunday's Berlin state election, the AfD party is polling just three points behind first place, according to a Sept. 10 survey conducted by German election research company Infratest-Dimap.

Machek, who also works for Europa Aeterna, which describes itself as a conservative political philosophy association rooted in Christianity, said the AfD is instilling a sense of patriotism and hope for the future. He sees Trump as a strong leader who also inspires national pride.
"I'm a Trump supporter from the beginning," said Machek. "It's a good sign. Just gives us hope that we're not alone."

The AfD fell just short of securing an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, but it still has a chance of becoming the first far-right party to hold state power since the Second World War. In Germany, governments are usually run by a coalition of parties, meaning the AfD will need co-operation from other political parties or individual elected representatives to govern.

blocks.text: AfD politicians cite Trump as the inspiration for some of their cultural policies, an area the party will control if it successfully forms government. They've even used the catchphrase "Make Saxony-Anhalt Great Again" on the campaign trail, an echo of Trump's MAGA slogan.
Although many AfD talking points pre-date Trump, the populist party is one of several around the world for which the U.S. president has provided a blueprint for how to gain mainstream support.

"Trump represents a model … of how you can whip up the base, how you can make electoral gains, and maybe even how you can seize power," said Eric Langenbacher, a political scientist with the American-German Institute in Washington, D.C.

"The fact that he's shown that what people thought were fantastical policies can actually be implemented, I think that is the biggest impact that he's had on the AfD, on Germany, and on many other countries as well."
AfD victory in Germany sparks protest, celebration
Hard line on immigration
Langenbacher said some of the AfD's strict immigration policies echo those implemented by the Trump administration.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD has said it wants to strip citizenship from immigrants who commit crimes, expand detention centres for deportees and create a "deportation task force," a term Trump started using during his 2016 presidential campaign.

"Sometimes, I feel like in Saxony-Anhalt, they just cut and paste from Project 2025," said Langenbacher, referring to the policy blueprint from the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think-tank, that has inspired some of Trump's efforts to reshape government and immigration enforcement.

The similarities between Trump and the AfD are evident to Anne-Christin Richter, 43, who lived and worked for a commercial vehicle manufacturer in Detroit for 10 years. She recently moved back to her hometown of Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt's capital.

Richter said her community feels more divided than when she left and though she can't attribute this directly to the AfD, she fears the party's anti-immigration rhetoric is fuelling racism in her community. Her daughters are both Black, and she says one of them was called a racial slur at a Magdeburg playground about a year ago. Richter said it happened when her daughter, now seven, tried standing up to an older child who was taunting immigrant children at the park.
A rise in racist rhetoric is something Richter said she also observed while living under Trump.
"You could see in the [Michigan] suburbs, suddenly, people started to say, ‘We don't want anybody to run around in our neighbourhood that's coloured,'" said Richter, whose boyfriend is Black.
"As soon as [Trump] was in power, everybody knew, ‘Now, we can say what we're really thinking,' right? And that's something I'm definitely afraid of."
AfD looks to revamp public buildings
If it successfully forms government in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD will control cultural and education policy, and it has said it will implement a widespread "patriotic shift" across society.

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is an AfD politician in Saxony-Anhalt who wrote the sections on education and culture in the party's manifesto. He told CBC News at an AfD event in mid-August that he's inspired by Trump.
"We will make Germany great again," said Tillschneider. "We will rebuild our wealth, our freedom, our liberty. Rejoice, please. Don't be afraid."

The AfD's manifesto proposes following the example of a first-term Trump executive order to promote classical architecture in public buildings. It has specifically singled out for criticism the world-renowned Bauhaus movement and one of its original, 100-year-old buildings, which used to be an architecture school, in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD's manifesto calls Bauhaus untraditional and unnationalistic.

Barbara Steiner, the CEO of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, said this kind of criticism predates Trump and has roots in the Nazi era, when the Bauhaus school was labelled "alien" and "lacking tradition." It closed under Nazi pressure in 1933 and reopened in Dessau in 1976 and is now a research, teaching and exhibition facility.
"It was wrong 100 years ago, and it is still wrong," Steiner said.

In its manifesto, the party also says it wants to revise history lessons in "all types of schools" to focus more on the country's achievements, arguing that emphasizing the negatives has caused Germans to harbour a "guilt complex" that damages national pride.

Trump has targeted cultural organizations using similar language. In March 2025, he signed an executive order claiming cultural organizations such as the Smithsonian Institution, which operates more than 20 museums, undermine U.S. achievements with negative ideologies.

"Rather than fostering unity and a deeper understanding of our shared past, the widespread effort to rewrite history deepens societal divides and fosters a sense of national shame," reads the executive order.

The AfD also promises to follow the U.S. in declaring Antifa, a decentralized anti-fascist movement, as a terrorist organization. It's something Trump signed into law as an executive order in September 2025.
Trump unpopular in Germany
Although numerous AfD supporters told CBC News they like Trump, polls suggest that the president is widely unpopular in Germany overall.

In March 2026, only 15 per cent of Germans considered the U.S. a reliable partner, according to Infratest-Dimap. That number climbed to 37 per cent among AfD supporters. Only one in eight Germans view Trump positively, according to a January 2026 survey from Infratest-Dimap.

Some AfD politicians may welcome praise from Trump as a boost to the party's visibility, said Thomas Greven, a political scientist at Berlin's Freie University, but supporting a foreign leader with an unpredictable agenda could backfire for the party.
"You don't want to be caught endorsing someone who is very obviously hurting your country's economy," said Greven.
Greven said AfD and MAGA are both inward-looking and ultra-nationalistic, making any long-term relationship tenuous, despite their perceived ideological closeness.
"The nationalism that unites them for this project will ultimately divide them and will divide nations."
